# Chronological Account: GPT-5 (high reasoning) Failure Behavior on GDPval

## Source

The reference points at Section 3.4 ("Increasing Reasoning Effort and Scaffolding") and Appendix A.3 ("Additional Detail on Prompt-Tuning") of the GDPval paper (arXiv 2510.04374), with relevant supporting context in §3.3 and §A.2.6. The "failure" in this reference is not a single trajectory but an aggregate behavioral pattern observed across many GDPval tasks before a prompt-tuning intervention was applied.

## Setup the agent ran in

- **Agent**: GPT-5 at high reasoning effort, running in a custom OpenAI harness with the **web search tool** and **code interpreter tool** enabled, sampled in the background. Several extra Python libraries were preinstalled into the container (listed in §A.6.4). The harness sampled each task 3 times per model.
- **Workload**: The GDPval gold subset — 220 real, economically valuable knowledge-work tasks spanning 44 occupations, with reference files (mean 1.92, max 38 per task) and required deliverable files (mean 1.54, max 36 per task). Tasks averaged ~9.5 expert hours and ~$398 in value, and 67.7% required interacting with at least one reference file. Deliverables included PDFs, PPTX, DOCX, XLSX, MP4, ZIP, etc.
- **Grading**: Blind pairwise comparisons by professional industry experts (3 graders per sample, 9 comparisons per prompt-model pair). A separate clustering pipeline categorized expert justifications for why a deliverable lost.

## What the agent did, step by step (aggregate behavior)

1. **Received a real-world task prompt plus reference files**, e.g., a request to produce a multi-page PDF, a slide deck, or a spreadsheet appropriate to a given occupation.
2. **Used the code interpreter and web search tools** to draft and assemble the deliverable inside the sandbox. The harness allowed background sampling and had pre-installed libraries to support file generation (e.g., for PDF/PPTX rendering).
3. **Generated the deliverable file(s)** in the requested format (PDF, PPTX, DOCX, XLSX, etc.) and submitted them along with deliverable text.
4. **Did not, in most runs, open or visually inspect the produced files before submitting.** Section 3.4 reports that prior to the prompt intervention, only **15%** of agent runs used multimodal capabilities to inspect deliverables; the intervention later raised this to **97%**, indicating that the baseline behavior was to ship the file without rendering it back as an image and looking at it.
5. **Submitted the deliverable**. The harness then handed the artifact off for expert grading.

## Signals / feedback received about the deliverables

Expert graders judged the deliverables against the human expert's solution and a clustering pipeline aggregated the rationales. The pattern that emerged for GPT-5 high (§3.3, §3.4):

- GPT-5 high "lost mainly from formatting errors" (in contrast to Claude/Grok/Gemini, which lost mostly to instruction-following failures).
- GPT-5 and Grok had the **fewest accuracy errors**, and GPT-5 had the **fewest instruction-following issues** — but all models "sometimes hallucinated data or miscalculated."
- §A.2.4 / Figure 12: Claude won on PDF, XLSX, and PPT deliverables; GPT-5 only led on pure-text outputs, "though overall win rates remain low."
- §A.2.6 / Figure 14: When experts re-rated GPT-5's losing deliverables for severity, the most common bucket was "acceptable but subpar"; ~29% were rated "bad" or "catastrophic" (≈3% catastrophic), and ~23% of failures were actually re-rated as model-better-than-human (within the inter-rater noise floor).

## Where things specifically went wrong

Two concrete, observable defects dominated the formatting-error category for GPT-5 high before the intervention (§3.4):

1. **Black-square artifacts inside generated PDFs** affecting **over half** of all PDFs GPT-5 produced. (The paper's prompt fix later instructs the agent to use LibreOffice rather than other PDF libraries, implying the artifacts stemmed from the chosen rendering library.)
2. **Egregious formatting errors in PowerPoint files in 86% of PPTX deliverables** — the Appendix A.3 prompt enumerates the failure surface: text or graphics "cut off, overlapping, distorted, blank, hard to read (dark text on dark background or light text on light background)," blank pages, slide-limit overruns, and overlapping graphics.

Additional smaller defects implied by the corrective prompt (§A.3):
- Use of the non-breaking-hyphen character ‑ (U+2011) and other non-standard Unicode/emoji/bullets that render poorly on some platforms.
- Diagrams or plots too small to be legible, or "complicated visuals constructed by overlaying shapes" that "appear unprofessional."
- Fonts not available across platforms and not embedded in the document.
- Putting deliverables "purely in the deliverable text" with links instead of submitting the actual files; excess verbosity; corrupted video files.
- Not declaring when part of a task was unsolvable (e.g., no internet).

The unifying behavioral root signal: the agent was **not rendering its own visual deliverables back as images and checking them** (15% rate of multimodal self-inspection), so visual defects passed through unnoticed.

## Final outcome

- On the gold subset, GPT-5 high's deliverables matched or beat the human expert on only a minority of tasks (Claude Opus 4.1 led at 47.6% wins+ties; GPT-5 was lower overall and only led on pure-text outputs).
- §3.4 then describes the **intervention** applied to this same agent:
  - A new prompt (full text in A.3) requiring 5 mandatory formatting-check steps: convert deliverables to PNGs with LibreOffice, display and visually scan them, run programmatic checks for blank/overlapping/cut-off content, summarize the prompt's deliverable instructions and match them against the file, and verify nothing is corrupted — re-running the loop until clean, then emitting a `CONFIDENCE[XX]` line.
  - Scaffolding changes: enabling GET requests in the container and best-of-N sampling with N=4 judged by a GPT-5 grader.
- After the intervention:
  - Black-square PDF artifacts were **fully eliminated**.
  - Egregious PPTX formatting errors fell from **86% → 64%**.
  - Multimodal self-inspection of deliverables rose from **15% → 97%**.
  - Human preference win rate rose by **~5 percentage points** (Figure 9b).

In other words, the observable failure of the unmodified GPT-5 high agent was that it produced functionally and substantively reasonable deliverables but submitted them with visible rendering/formatting defects — most strikingly black-square artifacts in PDFs and assorted overlap/cut-off/legibility errors in PowerPoint files — without ever having opened the artifact to look at it before handing it off.
